exercise1.prompt: When a Merge Goes Wrong: Join whatever type the ids arrived as

hiddenCases.name: a genuinely absent key still matches nothing

exercise1.hint: Convert both id columns with astype(str) on copies, then merge. Converting only one side leaves the mismatch exactly where it was.

exercise2.prompt: When a Merge Goes Wrong: Count the duplicate keys first
exercise2.hint: df["id"].duplicated().sum() counts the repeats on each side. Then merge and take len() — two duplicates each side give four rows, which is the multiplication this exercise is about.

questions.prompt: Duplicate keys on both sides of a merge do what to the row count?
choices: Multiply — every left match pairs with every right match
questions.explain: Two and two make four. This is how a join quietly inflates a total.

questions.prompt: A key is int in one table and str in the other. What does pd.merge do?
questions.explain: pandas refuses to join an int key to a text key, and says which column. The silent failure is two text keys that differ, like "007" and "7".

questions.prompt: Which argument makes pandas check the relationship you assumed?
questions.explain: It raises when the data disagrees, instead of silently multiplying rows.

questions.prompt: What is the cheapest check before a join?
choices: Compare the key dtypes and count duplicates on each side
questions.explain: Those two lines catch both of this lesson’s failures before they become a wrong number.
